title: Fly Me to the Moon
whyNotable: Bart Howard wrote it in 1954 as 'In Other Words', and the first commercial recording was Kaye Ballard's, issued by Decca in April 1954 and reviewed in Billboard that May. Sinatra's Count Basie/Quincy Jones recording came a decade later, in 1964, and swallowed the song's identity whole.

title: Hooked on a Feeling
whyNotable: B. J. Thomas recorded it first, released October 1968 on Scepter. Blue Swede's 1974 cover bolted on a chanted intro borrowed from a 1971 Jonathan King version, and Reservoir Dogs plus the Guardians of the Galaxy trailers made that arrangement the only one most listeners have ever heard.

title: I Can See Clearly Now
whyNotable: The reverse-direction trap: because Jimmy Cliff's Cool Runnings version is the one a generation grew up with, the song is often taken for a Jamaican reggae standard, when it was written and recorded by American singer Johnny Nash and was a US No. 1 in 1972.

title: If You Don't Know Me by Now
whyNotable: A Philly soul landmark sung by Teddy Pendergrass (No. 1 R&B, No. 3 pop, 1972) that a generation now hears as a Simply Red song after Mick Hucknall's 1989 US No. 1. Gamble and Huff originally wrote it for Labelle, who never recorded it.

title: It's All Over Now
whyNotable: Bobby Womack's group the Valentinos recorded it on 24 March 1964 for Sam Cooke's SAR label and reached only No. 94; the Stones cut theirs at Chess Studios on 10 June, releasing it on 26 June for their first UK No. 1. Barely three months separate the original from the version that erased it.

title: Kingston Town
whyNotable: UB40's signature ballad, a UK No. 4 and a No. 1 in France and the Netherlands, is a cover of Lord Creator's 1970 Clandisc single produced by Clancy Eccles - the same Labour of Love covers-project trap as their Red Red Wine.

title: Land of 1000 Dances
whyNotable: New Orleans R&B singer Chris Kenner wrote and first recorded it on Instant in 1962; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic cut (No. 6 pop, No. 1 R&B) is the best-known version and is widely assumed to be the original. The famous chanted hook belongs to neither - Cannibal & the Headhunters added it on their 1965 Rampart version.

title: Love Hurts
whyNotable: The Everly Brothers cut it first in July 1960 and buried it as an album track on A Date with the Everly Brothers - never a single. Nazareth's 1974 power-ballad rendition is the only version ever to be a US hit single, which is why the song reads as a Scottish hard-rock original.

title: Make You Feel My Love
whyNotable: Bob Dylan wrote it, but Billy Joel's recording (as 'To Make You Feel My Love', 13 August 1997) reached the public first, ahead of Dylan's own Time Out of Mind release on 30 September 1997. Adele's 2008 version, propelled by X Factor performances in 2010, is now widely assumed to be the song's origin.

title: Mustang Sally
whyNotable: Mack Rice wrote it and cut it himself as 'Sir Mack Rice' for Blue Rock in May 1965; Pickett's 1966 Atlantic version buried it so completely that the song is now treated as a Pickett original.

title: My Way
writer: Jacques Revaux (music); Claude François and Gilles Thibaut (original French lyrics); Paul Anka (English lyrics)
whyNotable: The definitive Sinatra signature song is an English rewrite of the French chanson 'Comme d'habitude', recorded and released by Claude François in November 1967. Paul Anka bought the adaptation rights after hearing the tune on French radio.

title: Papa Was a Rollin' Stone
whyNotable: Whitfield gave it to the Undisputed Truth first - single released 9 May 1972 on Gordy, a modest No. 63 pop - then re-cut it with the Temptations four months later for a Hot 100 No. 1 and three Grammys. Same label, same producer, and the first version is almost entirely forgotten.

title: Pass the Dutchie
writer: The Mighty Diamonds (adapted from Leroy Sibbles' 1968 instrumental 'Full Up')
whyNotable: Musical Youth's 1982 UK No. 1 is remembered as a novelty original, but it is a sanitised retitling of The Mighty Diamonds' 1981 'Pass the Kouchie'; a 2012 High Court case confirmed the two share the same copyright.

title: Rhinestone Cowboy
whyNotable: Writer Larry Weiss recorded it himself on his 1974 album Black and Blue Suite, where it made no commercial impact outside a No. 71 placing in Australia; Campbell's May 1975 version topped both the Hot 100 and the country chart and became his signature song.

title: Rivers of Babylon
whyNotable: One of the best-selling UK singles ever and universally filed as Euro-disco by Boney M., yet it was written and recorded in 1970 by Jamaican rocksteady group The Melodians for Leslie Kong, and reached the world via The Harder They Come.

title: Seasons in the Sun
whyNotable: Brel recorded the French original 'Le Moribond' on 22 February 1961, released that July. The Kingston Trio cut the first English version in 1963 using Rod McKuen's adaptation; Terry Jacks recorded his own reworking in Vancouver in 1973.

title: Seven Bridges Road
whyNotable: Country-folk songwriter Steve Young wrote and first recorded it for his 1969 A&M album Rock Salt & Nails; the Eagles' harmony live version, recorded 28 July 1980 and issued as a single that December, reached No. 21 and is now assumed to be an Eagles original.

title: Some Kind of Wonderful
whyNotable: John Ellison wrote it and cut it with his own R&B group Soul Brothers Six for Atlantic in 1967, where it stalled at No. 91. Grand Funk's December 1974 Capitol single hit No. 3, and the song is now heard as a rock original rather than a failed soul 45.

title: Sukiyaki
whyNotable: Released in Japan on 15 October 1961 as 'Ue o Muite Arukō', Kyu Sakamoto's record was renamed 'Sukiyaki' abroad. A Taste of Honey's 1981 version used entirely new English words, and 4 P.M.'s 1994 hit copied that arrangement, leaving two generations who never met the Japanese original.

title: Sway
originalArtist: Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta
writer: Luis Demetrio and Pablo Beltrán Ruiz (original); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
whyNotable: The Mexican bolero-mambo '¿Quién será?' was first recorded as an instrumental by Pablo Beltrán Ruiz y su Orquesta for RCA Victor in 1953. Dean Martin's Capitol single of 1954 carried Norman Gimbel's unrelated English lyric, and Michael Bublé's 2004 revival pushed the Spanish original further out of view.

title: Tennessee Waltz
originalArtist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
writer: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
whyNotable: Pee Wee King's band recorded it 2 December 1947 and RCA Victor released it in January 1948, a No. 3 country hit; Patti Page's November 1950 Mercury pop version spent nine weeks at No. 1 and eclipsed the country original entirely.

title: The Best
whyNotable: Bonnie Tyler released it first, in January 1988 from her album Hide Your Heart. Tina Turner's August 1989 Capitol cover - which added a bridge and a key change at her request - became the version used across decades of advertising and is near-universally taken for the original.

title: The First Cut Is the Deepest
whyNotable: Soul singer P. P. Arnold released the first recording on 21 April 1967 on Immediate, months before writer Cat Stevens issued his own version on New Masters (15 December 1967). Rod Stewart's 1977 hit and Sheryl Crow's 2003 version are what most listeners know, and the song's first voice was neither.

title: The Girl from Ipanema
writer: Antônio Carlos Jobim (music); Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
whyNotable: 'Garota de Ipanema' was written in 1962 and first commercially recorded that year by Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro. The Getz/Gilberto recording everyone treats as the original was taped in March 1963 and released on Verve in March 1964.

title: The House of the Rising Sun
whyNotable: The oldest known recording is the Appalachian duo Ashley and Foster's, cut 6 September 1933 for Vocalion. Guthrie, Lead Belly, Josh White, Baez, Simone and Dylan all recorded it before the Animals' June 1964 single, which the public treats as the song's point of origin.

title: The Lion Sleeps Tonight
writer: Solomon Linda (original); George David Weiss (English adaptation)
whyNotable: The a cappella Zulu record 'Mbube' was cut by Solomon Linda's group at Gallo's Johannesburg studio in 1939. It reached the West via Alan Lomax and The Weavers' 'Wimoweh' (1951) before The Tokens' RCA Victor single of October 1961 became the version the world credits - while Linda received essentially nothing.

title: The Tide Is High
whyNotable: Blondie's 1980 US and UK No. 1 is routinely treated as a Blondie song, but it is a cover of a 1967 Jamaican rocksteady single by The Paragons, written by their lead singer John Holt and cut for Duke Reid's Treasure Isle.
